articles.title: Finding your bearings
articles.summary: Anterior, posterior, medial, and lateral describe positions in the person’s brain.
paragraphs: Anterior points toward the face; posterior toward the back of the head. Superior is above and inferior below. Medial is toward the midline, lateral away from it. Left and right always refer to the person, even as you rotate the model.

In the forebrain, dorsal generally means superior and ventral inferior. The neuraxis bends: these terms change orientation in the brainstem and spinal cord. Ipsilateral means the same side; contralateral the opposite side.
articles.scope: A spatial vocabulary, not a separate structure. Use the orientation labels and View camera presets to relate these terms to the model.

explorations.note: Compare section planes in real human specimens, then relate their orientation to the model.

articles.title: The three section planes
articles.summary: Sagittal, coronal, and axial slices reveal different relationships inside the brain.
paragraphs: A sagittal plane separates left from right; the midsagittal plane passes through the midline. A coronal plane separates front from back. An axial, or horizontal, plane separates upper from lower portions.

Brain scans presents these three planes together. Its crosshairs locate one point in a population MRI template. The Anatomy cutaway clips a separate surface atlas; it is not a registered slice of that MRI.
articles.scope: The MRI template and 3D surface have different source data. A plane name describes orientation; it does not establish correspondence between those datasets.

explorations.note: Inspect linked axial, coronal, and sagittal slices of a real population template. Its coordinates are separate from this surface atlas.
See corresponding section orientations on human specimens.

articles.title: Gyri, sulci, and fissures
articles.summary: Raised folds and the grooves between them are the landmarks of the cortical surface.
paragraphs: A gyrus is a ridge of folded cortex; a sulcus is a groove. Fissure is used for some prominent grooves. The central sulcus lies between the precentral and postcentral gyri. The lateral, or Sylvian, fissure separates the temporal lobe from overlying frontal and parietal cortex.
Desikan–Killiany parcels follow anatomical conventions about these folds. A parcel includes the exposed ridge and adjacent banks down into neighboring sulci.
articles.scope: Grooves are visible in the surface geometry but do not have separate selectable meshes. Folding patterns and parcel borders vary between people.

articles.title: Gray matter and white matter
articles.summary: Two tissue compartments with different cellular organization, both containing neurons’ processes and glia.
paragraphs: Gray matter includes cell bodies, dendrites, synapses, axons, and glia. It forms cortical sheets and deep nuclei. White matter contains many myelinated axons together with supporting cells; it lies beneath the cerebral cortex.
The cerebral white matter meshes show segmented tissue compartments. They do not reconstruct individual axons, their direction, or their cortical endpoints.
articles.scope: The tissue colors are a visualization choice. A mesh’s apparent thickness and smoothness are limited by its MRI segmentation and surface processing.

explorations.note: Inspect tissue contrast in a population average; this image is not a microscopic tissue classification.
Cortical and subcortical fiber anatomy on real specimens; individual axons are not resolved.

articles.title: The coverings around the brain
articles.summary: Dura, arachnoid, and pia form distinct coverings around the central nervous system.
paragraphs: From outside inward, the meninges are dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater. The tough dura forms supporting folds, including the falx between the cerebral hemispheres and the tentorium over the cerebellum. The arachnoid spans surface grooves; the pia closely follows the brain’s contours.

CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia. Wider parts of this space are called cisterns. A pial surface mesh describes a boundary of brain tissue; it does not reconstruct the pia, arachnoid, dura, or their spaces as separate layers.
articles.scope: Meninges, skull, falx, tentorium, cisterns, and dural sinuses are not modeled. The cortex and cerebellum links provide spatial landmarks beneath those coverings.

explorations.note: Unfixed human tissue and its coverings; broader specimen context, not a verified separate demonstration of every meningeal layer.

articles.title: Following cerebrospinal fluid
articles.summary: Ventricular cavities connect with fluid spaces around the brain and spinal cord.
paragraphs: Much CSF is secreted by the choroid plexus. The classical ventricular route runs from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina to the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth, then through its apertures into subarachnoid spaces. CSF provides buoyant support and a regulated fluid environment.

Classical descriptions include outflow associated with arachnoid granulations and nerve sheaths. Research also identifies meningeal lymphatic vessels. The ventricular sequence does not quantify exchange with brain tissue or the contribution of each clearance route.

Absinta and colleagues visualized dural lymphatic vessels with specialized contrast-enhanced MRI in five healthy human volunteers and three marmosets, with supporting tissue evidence. That study demonstrated vessels; it did not establish a complete human CSF flow map.
articles.scope: This atlas shows selected ventricular compartments and lateral-ventricular plexus. The small foramina, aqueduct, apertures, subarachnoid spaces, and lymphatic vessels lack separate meshes. No fluid motion, direction, pressure, or flow rate is measured here.

explorations.note: Four stops through existing plexus and ventricular meshes. This is an anatomical learning sequence, not a fluid simulation.
Compare ventricular spaces in three linked population-template slices. These structural images do not measure CSF flow.
Human specimen sections, casts, and diagrams showing ventricular anatomy. Opens the institutional film on its original channel.

articles.title: Two different blood–brain interfaces
articles.summary: The vascular blood–brain barrier and the choroid-plexus blood–CSF barrier occupy different cell layers.
paragraphs: At most brain microvessels, specialized endothelial cells and their tight junctions restrict movement between blood and neural tissue. Selective transport systems regulate exchange. Supporting interactions with neighboring cells help maintain this blood–brain barrier; it is not an impermeable wall or a visible membrane around an entire brain region.

The choroid plexus has fenestrated capillaries. Its blood–CSF barrier is instead formed by junctions between choroid epithelial cells. These two interfaces therefore separate different compartments at different anatomical locations. Arachnoid barrier cells form another interface around the subarachnoid compartment.
articles.scope: Neither endothelial junctions, choroid epithelial junctions, transporters, nor barrier permeability are modeled. A plexus mesh represents gross tissue, not its microscopic barrier.

explorations.note: Ventricular and plexus context on real specimens; a gross dissection does not resolve endothelial or epithelial tight junctions.

articles.title: How blood reaches the brain
articles.summary: Internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems supply overlapping, variable arterial territories.
paragraphs: The internal carotid system gives rise to anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Broadly, ACA branches supply much medial frontal and parietal cortex, while MCA branches supply much of the lateral hemisphere. Small penetrating branches supply deep structures; a surface view alone cannot describe this distribution.

The vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery. This posterior system supplies brainstem and cerebellar territories and gives rise to posterior cerebral arteries supplying much occipital and inferomedial temporal cortex. Communicating arteries connect anterior and posterior systems around the circle of Willis.

These are broad anatomical patterns. Arterial branching, collateral connections, and territorial boundaries vary. A cortical parcel is not an arterial territory, and a population MRI template is not an angiogram.
articles.scope: No arteries, capillaries, perfusion maps, or individual vascular territories are segmented. The linked cortex, deep structures, and brainstem are context landmarks; their highlight does not claim a measured blood supply.

explorations.note: Use structural MRI for regional orientation. No MR angiography, arterial labeling, or blood-flow measurements are included in this template.

articles.title: Veins, sinuses, and lymphatics
articles.summary: Venous blood and lymphatic drainage involve different vessels around and within the brain.
paragraphs: Superficial and deep cerebral veins collect blood from different parts of the brain and communicate through venous networks. Cerebral veins drain into venous sinuses within the dura. These channels differ from the arteries supplying the tissue; cerebral veins do not generally run alongside matching arteries.

Deep venous drainage includes the internal cerebral veins and great cerebral vein. Major dural channels include the sagittal, straight, transverse, and sigmoid sinuses, with outflow toward internal jugular veins. Their arrangement and relative size vary.

Dural lymphatic vessels are distinct from these blood-filled sinuses. Human and marmoset MRI and histology in the Absinta study identified lymphatic vessels near dural sinuses. Proximity to a sinus does not make the vessel a vein or measure its drainage rate.
articles.scope: Veins, dural sinuses, jugular veins, and meningeal lymphatics are not reconstructed. Related meshes provide landmarks only. Neither the 3D model nor the bundled structural templates is a venogram or lymphatic-flow study.

articles.title: Brainstem levels and landmarks
articles.summary: Midbrain, pons, and medulla connect the forebrain, cerebellum, and spinal cord.
paragraphs: The brainstem continues from the diencephalon above to the spinal cord below. Ascending and descending axons pass through it, alongside nuclei that process cranial-nerve information. A surface landmark and an internal nucleus are different things: locating a bulge does not identify every cell group beneath it.

In a section, distinguish fiber bundles from gray-matter nuclei and nearby CSF spaces. The cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain; the fourth ventricle lies behind the pons and upper medulla. Pontine connections reach the cerebellum through the middle cerebellar peduncles.

Medullary networks contribute to breathing, swallowing, and cardiovascular regulation. These functions involve multiple connected nuclei and pathways; the single outer brainstem mesh does not resolve them.

rows.label: Midbrain
rows.summary: Between the diencephalon and pons.
rows.detail: Cerebral peduncles anteriorly; colliculi in the posterior tectum; substantia nigra, red nucleus, and periaqueductal gray internally.

rows.label: Pons
rows.summary: Between midbrain and medulla, in front of the cerebellum.
rows.detail: A prominent ventral base and internal tegmentum; pontine fibers connect with the cerebellum.

rows.label: Medulla
rows.summary: Between pons and spinal cord.
rows.detail: Ventral pyramids contain descending corticospinal fibers; many cross near the cord. The inferior olive is a nearby landmark.

articles.scope: Only one brainstem surface is segmented here. Midbrain, pons, medulla, nuclei, peduncles, long tracts, and cranial-nerve roots are not separate selectable meshes. The fourth ventricle and cerebellar compartments are available as neighboring anatomy, not internal brainstem labels.

explorations.note: A UBC laboratory overview using specimens and diagrams. Compare its visible landmarks with the unsplit brainstem model.
Compare brainstem, cerebellum, and fourth-ventricle relationships in linked population-template slices. Small nuclei and individual nerves are not labeled.

articles.title: The twelve cranial nerves
articles.summary: Compare sensory, motor, and parasympathetic roles with their central connections.
paragraphs: The conventional twelve pairs carry different combinations of sensory and motor information. “Mixed” means a nerve includes both sensory and motor components; parasympathetic fibers are an autonomic motor component. The comparison gives selected principal roles, not every branch, target, or reflex.

Forebrain connections of I and II differ from the brainstem associations of most other cranial nerves. XI has an important spinal motor component. A nerve’s surface attachment is not a complete map of its nuclei: sensory systems can extend across several brainstem levels.

rows.label: I · Olfactory
rows.summary: Sensory · smell.
rows.detail: Olfactory receptor axons reach the olfactory bulb; this is not a brainstem attachment.

rows.label: II · Optic
rows.summary: Sensory · vision.
rows.detail: Retinal fibers pass through the optic nerve, chiasm, and tract toward forebrain targets.

rows.label: III · Oculomotor
rows.summary: Motor + parasympathetic · most eye movements and intrinsic eye-muscle control.
rows.detail: Emerges from the anterior midbrain in the interpeduncular fossa.

rows.label: IV · Trochlear
rows.summary: Motor · superior oblique eye muscle.
rows.detail: Emerges from the dorsal midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus.

rows.label: V · Trigeminal
rows.summary: Mixed · facial sensation and chewing muscles.
rows.detail: Attaches to the anterolateral pons through a large sensory and smaller motor root.

rows.label: VI · Abducens
rows.summary: Motor · lateral rectus, which turns the eye outward.
rows.detail: Emerges at the pons–medulla junction, near the midline.

rows.label: VII · Facial
rows.summary: Mixed + parasympathetic · facial expression, taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, tear and salivary secretion.
rows.detail: Motor, sensory, and autonomic components travel together; the nerve attaches near the pons–medulla junction.

rows.label: VIII · Vestibulocochlear
rows.summary: Sensory · hearing and head motion/balance.
rows.detail: Cochlear and vestibular components carry inner-ear input at the pons–medulla junction.

rows.label: IX · Glossopharyngeal
rows.summary: Mixed + parasympathetic · posterior tongue taste, pharyngeal sensation, stylopharyngeus, and parotid secretion.
rows.detail: Medullary pathways include solitary, ambiguus, and inferior salivatory nuclei.

rows.label: X · Vagus
rows.summary: Mixed + parasympathetic · throat/larynx motor pathways, visceral sensation, and autonomic supply to thoracic and abdominal organs.
rows.detail: Medullary components include ambiguus, solitary, and dorsal vagal motor nuclei.

rows.label: XI · Accessory
rows.summary: Motor · sternocleidomastoid and trapezius for head turning and shoulder elevation.
rows.detail: Its spinal motor component arises from an upper cervical cell column, rather than only the brainstem.

rows.label: XII · Hypoglossal
rows.summary: Motor · tongue movements.
rows.detail: Rootlets emerge between the medullary pyramid and olive.

articles.scope: There are no individual cranial-nerve, root, ganglion, or cranial-nerve-nucleus meshes in this atlas. Opening the brainstem shows its overall location, not the course of a selected nerve. The comparison is an anatomical reference, not a clinical examination guide.

explorations.note: UTHealth’s laboratory links this cranial-nerve and vessel dissection. Inspect specimen attachments; this does not add nerve meshes or verified timestamps to the atlas.
Utah’s brainstem lesson combines human specimens and reflex demonstrations. Gross views do not resolve every nerve nucleus.

articles.title: Cerebellar lobes and connections
articles.summary: Relate the folded cortex, vermis, white matter, deep nuclei, and three pairs of peduncles.
paragraphs: The cerebellum lies behind the brainstem. A midline vermis joins two hemispheres. Its tightly folded cortex surrounds white matter and deep nuclei. The primary fissure separates anterior and posterior lobes; the posterolateral fissure marks off the flocculonodular lobe.

Three paired peduncles connect it with the brainstem. The middle peduncle brings pontine input. The inferior peduncle carries important medullary and spinal connections, with some outgoing fibers. The superior peduncle is a major route out of the cerebellar nuclei and also carries some input.

Functional divisions cut across simple lobe names: vestibulocerebellar circuits support gaze and balance; spinocerebellar circuits integrate body feedback with movement; cerebrocerebellar loops involve lateral hemispheres and cerebral cortex. These are broad circuit descriptions, not exact boundaries of a single task.

Dentate, interposed (emboliform and globose), and fastigial nuclei lie in the interior. They receive inhibitory Purkinje-cell output and participate in routes back to brainstem and forebrain motor systems. Some Purkinje cells instead project directly to vestibular nuclei outside the cerebellum.
articles.scope: The model separates left/right cerebellar cortex and white-matter compartments. It does not separately segment the vermis, individual lobes or lobules, deep nuclei, or peduncles. Smoothing and atlas sampling limit visible folial detail; a finer compartment surface is not a cellular or lobular atlas.

explorations.note: Utah’s lesson inspects cerebellar surfaces and peduncles, with clinical examples. These specimen landmarks are finer than the model’s compartment labels.
A UBC cerebellar anatomy laboratory lesson with specimens and diagrams. Opens at the beginning on the original channel.
Place the cerebellar stop within a selected motor-system learning sequence. This is not a measured tract or signal animation.

articles.title: Inside the cerebellar circuit
articles.summary: Three cortical layers transform mossy- and climbing-fiber input into Purkinje-cell output.
paragraphs: From surface inward, cerebellar cortex has a molecular layer, a Purkinje-cell layer, and a granular layer. Granule-cell axons rise and split into parallel fibers that excite Purkinje dendrites. Golgi, basket, and stellate interneurons add local interactions to this simplified account.

Mossy fibers bring varied spinal, pontine, vestibular, and other brainstem input through granule cells. Climbing fibers originate in the inferior olive and strongly excite Purkinje cells. Both input systems also send connections to deep nuclei.

Purkinje neurons provide the cortex’s inhibitory output to deep cerebellar nuclei, with direct vestibular-nucleus projections from some regions. Deep nuclei therefore combine incoming excitation with cortical inhibition. The cortical output and the output of the whole cerebellum are different stages.

The cerebellum contributes to adaptive movement and learning. Relating climbing-fiber signals and synaptic change to learning is a physiological model supported by experiments; the 3D compartment surfaces here do not measure spikes, synapses, or a person’s learning.
articles.scope: This is a written circuit explanation, not measured connectivity or simulated neural activity. Cellular layers, neurons, inferior olive, deep nuclei, and individual mossy/climbing fibers have no separate meshes. The cerebellar white-matter surface is a tissue compartment, not a reconstruction of these axons.

explorations.note: Orient the gross cerebellum on a specimen before reading its microscopic circuit. The film is not cellular imaging of these synapses.

articles.title: Inside the basal ganglia
articles.summary: Separate striatum, pallidum, and lentiform names, then match their subdivisions to the gross meshes available.
paragraphs: The basal ganglia are a set of connected nuclei, rather than one continuous mass. Their components occupy the cerebral hemispheres, diencephalon, and midbrain. They influence motor, associative, and limbic circuits; a single movement label does not describe their full role.

Caudate and putamen form the dorsal striatum. The nucleus accumbens belongs to ventral striatum; the selectable accumbens label is not the whole ventral striatal territory. Putamen and globus pallidus are grouped anatomically as the lentiform nucleus, even though they occupy different circuit stages.

Coronal sections expose relationships that the outer cortical surface hides. The internal capsule separates much of the caudate from putamen, with gray-matter bridges between them. The pallidum lies medial to putamen. The linked human specimen lessons show these gross relationships.

The eight model links below are bilateral caudate, putamen, pallidum, and accumbens labels. Finer mode improves surface sampling within a label. It does not divide pallidum into internal and external segments or reveal cell classes.
articles.scope: Cerebra has one globus pallidus mesh per hemisphere, without separate GPi or GPe. Subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra, accumbens core/shell, and individual internal-capsule fiber bundles have no separate selectable meshes. The ventral diencephalon composite label and whole brainstem are not precise substitutes for those nuclei. The table distinguishes anatomical names from the geometry actually available.

articles.title: Basal ganglia circuits and movement evidence
articles.summary: Follow selected direct, indirect, and hyperdirect relationships while separating a teaching model from recorded activity.
paragraphs: Basal ganglia circuits influence cortical and brainstem motor systems rather than forming a separate descending motor tract. In the selected motor loop, cortical input reaches striatum, and GPi or substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) sends inhibitory output toward thalamic targets. Other loops and projections also exist.

The table follows selected connection signs. Inhibition of an inhibitory output can release its target from inhibition: disinhibition. This account omits many cell types, collateral branches, recurrent connections, and timing effects. It should not be read as a complete wiring diagram or a binary action switch.

Nambu and colleagues (2000) electrically stimulated motor and somatosensory cortex in awake monkeys while recording subthalamic and pallidal neurons. Early excitation appeared in STN before pallidum; suppressing STN activity abolished the evoked pallidal excitations. This supported a rapid cortical route through STN. These are stimulation and spike-recording findings in monkeys, not a human activity map.

Cui and colleagues (2013) used genetically targeted GCaMP3 calcium signals and fiber optics in mice performing an operant task. Both direct- and indirect-pathway striatal populations showed transient activity increases around action initiation. This challenges an account in which one population must simply turn off whenever the other turns on. Population calcium signals do not resolve every neuron or establish a complete causal theory of human movement.
articles.scope: This is a written explanation of selected motor-loop relationships. No projection fibers, D1/D2 cell populations, dopamine concentrations, or electrical/calcium traces are modeled. The whole pallidum and thalamus meshes do not separate the nuclei or cells in these routes. The movement guide is an anatomical sequence, and the MRI link is structural contrast; neither reproduces the cited experiments. Ventral striatal circuits are outside this selected account.

comparison.caption: Selected motor-loop routes — written relationships, not modeled fibers

rows.label: Direct pathway
rows.summary: Striatum inhibits GPi/SNr, which inhibits its output targets.
rows.detail: Reducing that output can disinhibit thalamic targets. This is a connection-sign account, not a guarantee that every movement is facilitated.

rows.label: Indirect pathway
rows.summary: Striatum inhibits GPe; reduced GPe inhibition can release STN, which excites GPi/SNr.
rows.detail: This selected route can increase inhibitory output. GPe also projects directly to output nuclei; the displayed sequence omits other connections.

rows.label: Hyperdirect route
rows.summary: Cortex → STN → pallidum bypasses the striatal stage.
rows.detail: Awake-monkey stimulation and recordings supported rapid excitation along this route. This is not a measured fiber overlay in Cerebra.

rows.label: Nigrostriatal dopamine
rows.summary: SNc dopamine modulates striatal neurons, including populations associated with D1 and D2 receptors.
rows.detail: The classical account associates D1 with direct-pathway and D2 with indirect-pathway neurons. Dopamine modulation is more complex than a single excitatory or inhibitory wire.

rows.label: Concurrent pathway activity
rows.summary: Direct- and indirect-pathway population calcium signals both increased around action initiation in mice.
rows.detail: The Cui study measured activity-related fluorescence during behavior; it did not image these human meshes or show that every neuron in a pathway acts identically.

explorations.note: Visit selected cortical, basal-ganglia, thalamic, and cerebellar structures. This guide is not a direct/indirect pathway animation.

articles.title: Thalamic nuclei and atlas boundaries
articles.summary: Distinguish selected sensory, motor, and association nuclei from the gross thalamus labels displayed in 3D.
paragraphs: The two thalami lie beside the third ventricle. In the source segmentation definition, the internal capsule forms a lateral boundary and the lateral ventricle a superior boundary. These relationships help orient a gross view; they do not reveal each internal nucleus.

The internal medullary lamina separates major nuclear groups. Selected names below describe different connections, rather than interchangeable pieces of a uniform relay. Most nuclei cannot be identified reliably on a gross specimen slice without additional anatomical information.

FreeSurfer’s documented thalamus-proper definition excludes the lateral and medial geniculate bodies. Its ventral-diencephalon convention groups several neighboring territories, including geniculate regions. Cerebra’s composite label does not outline either geniculate nucleus separately. A biological name and an imaging label therefore need not cover the same territory.

Iglesias and colleagues’ 2018 atlas used serial histology of 12 thalami from six postmortem donors, with 26 nuclei delineated under its protocol and ex vivo MRI used for reconstruction. The specialized FreeSurfer nuclei module uses histological atlas information to estimate internal labels from MRI. Those atlas assets and subdivisions have not been applied to Cerebra’s gross meshes or structural templates.
articles.scope: There is one gross thalamus-proper mesh per hemisphere. Anterior, mediodorsal, VA/VL, VPL/VPM, pulvinar, intralaminar, geniculate, and reticular nuclei have no individual selectable meshes. Finer mode refines the outer surface of the existing label; it does not add nuclear boundaries. The third-ventricle and ventral-diencephalon links provide neighboring context. This selected comparison is not an exhaustive list of thalamic nuclei or a histological atlas.

rows.detail: The table selects this major relationship; it does not enumerate every VPM subdivision or input.

rows.label: Pulvinar

rows.detail: Its internal subdivisions are not distinguished by the gross mesh.

rows.label: Intralaminar nuclei · CM / Pf

rows.detail: Mouse recordings show state-dependent differences. It is not the brainstem reticular formation, and has no separate mesh here.

articles.title: Thalamus, cortex, and attention
articles.summary: Separate driver/modulator terminology from mouse experiments on reticular subnetworks and mediodorsal–prefrontal interactions.
paragraphs: Sherman and Guillery’s 1998 framework distinguishes inputs that convey a sensory receptive-field signal (drivers) from inputs that alter its transmission (modulators). It also distinguishes ascending first-order relays from higher-order routes receiving cortical driving input. These are functional ideas about particular connections, not colors or subdivisions visible on the gross thalamus mesh.

Their sensory examples separate cortical layer-5 driving routes from layer-6 modulatory feedback. The paper explicitly discusses limits to applying these criteria where receptive fields are not defined. A connection’s origin or transmitter alone is not a complete explanation of its function.

Halassa and colleagues (2014) combined neuronal ensemble recordings, behavioral testing, and connectivity-based optogenetic tagging in mice. Sensory-projecting reticular neurons participated in sleep spindles and changed their activity during attention, differently from limbic-projecting neurons. Targeted optical manipulations changed task performance. The findings support state-dependent inhibitory subnetworks, rather than one uniform gate that is simply open or closed.

Schmitt and colleagues (2017) studied mice using rules to attend to visual or auditory targets. Neuronal recordings and optogenetic manipulations supported a mediodorsal-thalamus contribution to sustaining prefrontal rule representations. In that task, the mediodorsal signal was not itself a categorical copy of the rule. The result concerns a defined mouse experiment, not every human attentional state.

Anatomical projections, neuronal spike recordings, behavioral performance, and statistical fMRI contrasts are different kinds of evidence. The bundled human activity maps do not reproduce either mouse experiment, and a highlighted thalamus does not measure attention, sensory gating, or sleep.
articles.scope: This written account selects concepts and experiments; it is not a measured connectome or simulation. No individual thalamic nuclei, reticular shell, cortical layers, axons, spike trains, sleep recordings, or optogenetic data are rendered. The model links identify gross human atlas labels, not the experimental mouse structures. Guided paths provide anatomical context, and the MRI template has structural contrast without these nuclear boundaries.

articles.title: Inside the hippocampal formation
articles.summary: Locate the medial temporal structures, distinguish their internal names, and understand why a whole hippocampus mesh is not a subfield atlas.
paragraphs: The hippocampal formation commonly includes the dentate gyrus, hippocampus proper (cornu ammonis, or CA fields), and subicular cortex. It lies in each medial temporal lobe beside the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. Entorhinal cortex provides an adjacent cortical interface.

Coronal sections are useful for separating the hippocampus from the more anterior amygdala and nearby temporal cortex. Their appearance changes as the section moves from front to back. Use the linked specimen lessons and MRI for orientation; a single section cannot show the full folded structure.

Subfield boundaries depend on anatomical definitions, image contrast, and the labeling protocol. The 2015 Iglesias atlas used ultra-high-resolution postmortem human MRI. Its labels include territories absent from this model, and its CA2/3 label combines two named fields. A protocol label is not proof that those fields are biologically identical.

FreeSurfer cautions that internal subregion boundaries estimated from standard 1 mm T1 scans can depend strongly on atlas prior knowledge. Higher-resolution output labels do not themselves create new measured image detail. The bundled MRI templates have no hippocampal subfield labels.
articles.scope: Cerebra has one hippocampus mesh per hemisphere plus separate entorhinal and parahippocampal surface parcels. Dentate gyrus, CA fields, subicular territories, alveus, fimbria, and fornix have no separate selectable meshes. The gross hippocampus label should not be read as a precise outline of every component of the formation. Finer mode refines its surface, not these subdivisions.

articles.title: Hippocampal circuits and memory evidence
articles.summary: Separate a simplified anatomical route from experiments on synaptic plasticity and human memory impairment.
paragraphs: A common teaching sequence runs from entorhinal cortex through dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1. Subicular outputs reach entorhinal cortex and routes through the fornix. This selected route is not a complete wiring diagram of the hippocampal formation.

Bliss and Lømo’s 1973 experiment stimulated the perforant path and recorded extracellular population responses in the dentate area of anaesthetized rabbits. Fifteen of eighteen rabbits showed potentiation lasting from 30 minutes to 10 hours after conditioning stimulation. This was an experimentally evoked physiological change, not a recording of a human autobiographical memory.

Rempel-Clower and colleagues’ 1996 report combined neuropsychological testing with postmortem anatomy in three additional people with hippocampal damage, alongside earlier cases. Damage concentrated in bilateral CA1 could impair formation of new memories; more extensive damage could produce greater impairment. The cases differed in lesion extent and memory findings. They do not assign every kind of memory to one field.

Anatomical pathways, electrical recordings, behavioral tests, and MRI answer different questions. The selected memory learning path introduces several related regions; it does not animate information flow or reproduce either experiment. A statistical task map is also different from a synaptic recording.
articles.scope: The atlas contains no individual hippocampal neurons, synapses, pathway fibers, evoked potentials, or simulation of memory formation. The links below open gross anatomical context. Neither a teal highlight nor a finer mesh demonstrates potentiation, explains an individual’s memory ability, or reproduces a lesion study.

articles.title: Inside the cortical sheet
articles.summary: Most cerebral cortex has six cellular layers; a surface parcel does not show those layers.
paragraphs: Neocortex is conventionally described in six layers, numbered I at the pial surface through VI beside the white matter. Their cell densities, shapes, and connections differ. Layer IV is prominent in many sensory areas; superficial and deep layers have different projection patterns. This is a general organization, not a uniform wiring diagram.

Not all cortex follows the same six-layer pattern. Hippocampal and other allocortical territories have different organization. Layer boundaries and cell types require microscopic or molecular evidence, rather than a gyral name alone.

Langseth and colleagues combined in situ sequencing with single-nucleus reference types to map 59,816 cells in sampled human cortical tissue. Such cell maps operate at a different scale from this MRI-derived surface.
articles.scope: None of the six layers is individually modeled here. Loading a finer parcel increases mesh resolution; it does not reveal cellular layers or add histological evidence.

explorations.note: Gross cortical localization on human specimens. This film does not reveal the six microscopic cortical layers.

articles.title: A neuron’s working parts
articles.summary: Cell body, dendrites, axon, and terminals provide different parts of neuronal communication.
paragraphs: The soma contains the nucleus and much of the machinery maintaining a neuron. Dendrites and their spines receive many synaptic inputs. An axon carries signals toward terminals that communicate with other cells. The initial segment is a common site where action potentials begin.
This is a useful starting pattern, not a shape shared by every neuron. Branching, targets, electrical properties, and transmitter systems differ across neuronal classes.
articles.scope: Cells and their processes are below this model’s resolution. The related regions are places containing neurons, not reconstructions of individual cells.

articles.title: Glia: the other cellular partners
articles.summary: Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells have distinct roles.
paragraphs: Astrocytes help regulate the extracellular chemical environment and take up neurotransmitters. Oligodendrocytes make central nervous system myelin. Microglia participate in immune responses and clearance of cellular debris. Ependymal cells line the ventricles; their cilia contribute to movement of ventricular fluid.
These are broad families. Molecular studies distinguish further types and states within neuronal and non-neuronal populations.
articles.scope: No glial cells or ependymal layer are segmented. A ventricular mesh outlines a fluid compartment, not its microscopic lining.

articles.title: Myelin and rapid conduction
articles.summary: Insulating axon segments changes how an electrical signal travels along a fiber.
paragraphs: Myelin reduces membrane capacitance along insulated axon segments. Depolarization spreads between gaps called nodes, where voltage-gated channels regenerate the action potential. This node-to-node renewal is called saltatory conduction.

Oligodendrocytes form myelin in the central nervous system. White matter is rich in myelinated axons, but its surface mesh cannot show which individual axons are myelinated or how quickly they conduct.
articles.scope: This explanation describes a mechanism. The atlas has no electrical simulation, individual fibers, myelin measurements, or measured conduction speeds.

articles.title: How synapses pass a signal
articles.summary: Chemical transmission links presynaptic release to receptors on another cell.
paragraphs: At a typical chemical synapse, terminal depolarization opens calcium channels. Calcium entry promotes vesicle fusion and transmitter release. Transmitter acts on receptors across the synaptic cleft, changing the receiving cell’s electrical or biochemical state.

Excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic responses influence whether a neuron fires. Their effects depend on receptors, ion gradients, timing, and the other inputs arriving at that cell. A connection between regions does not specify all these mechanisms.
articles.scope: Synapses are not resolved in these meshes. Region connections are educational associations, not a measured synaptic wiring diagram or a simulation of thought.

articles.title: What counts as a brain cell type?
articles.summary: Shape, physiology, gene expression, and location reveal different aspects of cellular identity.
paragraphs: Siletti and colleagues profiled more than three million nuclei from adult human brain tissue. Their 2023 study reported 461 clusters and 3,313 subclusters, organized largely along developmental divisions. Those numbers describe a particular transcriptomic classification, not a final universal count of cell types.

RNA-based grouping helps distinguish populations that a large anatomical label combines. Sampling, analysis, species, age, and cell state matter when comparing taxonomies. The Allen Institute provides the human atlas data and its hierarchy for further exploration.
articles.scope: This reference links to human research; it does not import those cells into the 3D atlas. Cell classes are not assigned to individual mesh vertices, and mouse data must not be presented as measured human anatomy.

articles.title: What an atlas boundary means
articles.summary: A parcel is a region defined by a particular labeling method, with a particular resolution.
paragraphs: FreeSurfer’s Desikan–Killiany atlas divides the cortical surface using gyral anatomy and a learned labeling procedure. Its parcels are not equivalent to Brodmann’s cellular areas or to a functional map measured during a task.

Cerebra displays 68 cortical parcels plus 36 other segmented parts. A finer model adds geometric faces from a higher-resolution source surface. It does not add new internal structures, prove a functional boundary, or describe every individual’s anatomy.
articles.scope: Surface anatomy, cellular organization, and task activation are distinct measurements. The MRI templates, task maps, and surface model here come from separate sources; their spatial correspondence is not established by opening them in the same site.

articles.title: Common names and functional areas
articles.summary: Heschl’s gyrus, Broca’s area, and V1 do not all name the same kind of anatomical object.
paragraphs: A named gyrus describes a fold. A cytoarchitectonic area describes cellular organization. A functional area is characterized through physiological or behavioral evidence. Their borders need not coincide.

Structure search recognizes common names and shows the corresponding available parcels. Broca searches lead to the classical left inferior frontal landmarks; these parcels do not delineate an entire language system. Search notes explain each mapping and link its source.
articles.scope: Search aliases are navigation aids. They never create missing geometry or assert that a full parcel has one exclusive function.
